[[File:Eryngium campestre MHNT.BOT.2007.40.36.jpg|thumb|''Eryngium campestre'' - [[MHNT]]]]

'''''Eryngium campestre''''', known as '''field eryngo''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|accessdate=17 October 2014  |df=dmy-all}}</ref> or '''Watling Street thistle''',<ref name=Collins/> is a [[species]] of ''[[Eryngium]]'', which is also used medicinally.  A member of the carrot family [[Apiaceae]], it is a hairless, greenish [[perennial]] plant with tough spiny leaves.

==Description==
''Eryngium campestre'' is a stiff, greyish or greenish, hairless perennial, with complexly-divided prickly leaves, and a wide display of small greenish heads, each based with a whorl of 5-6 large spine-like bracts, and within a head each small flower is attended by a small simple spine. The basal leaves are long-stalked and [[pinnate]].

It has two natural varieties - <ref name="FOT">{{cite book |title=Flora of Turkey and the East Aegean Islands, vol. 4 |author=PH Davis |date=1972}}</ref>

''var. campestre'' is blueish-greyish green with the bracts (whorled under the heads) being widest near their middle, and geographically is more northern, stretching north of the Mediterranean from Portugal to Germany on the west side through to Turkey into Central European Russia on the east, with presence on the south in North Africa just in Algeria and Morocco.<ref name="PoWo-c">[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77230009-1 Plants of the World Online (with map)]</ref>

''var. virens (Link) Weins'' is yellowier-greeny with the bracts (whorled under the heads) being widest near their base, more dry-tolerant ([[xerophyte|xerophytic]]), and geographically is more southern and eastern, stretching along the south of the Mediterranean from Morocco to Iran, with patchy distribution directly on the north side.<ref name="PoWo-v">[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:77250229-1 Plants of the World Online (with map)]</ref>

In Britain it resembles the better known [[sea holly]] (''Eryngium maritimum''), but is taller and looser, greener, and the whorls under the flower heads are not leaf-like, the heads being smaller, or some of the garden Eryngos, but green. This plant flowers between July and September.<ref name=Collins>{{cite book |last1=McClintock |first1=David |last2=Fitter |first2=R.S.R. |year=1961 |title=The Pocket Guide to Wild Flowers |publisher=Collins |location=London |page=93 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is common in many places of its range but in Germany it is restricted to dry habitats near the Rivers [[Rhine]] and [[Elbe]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Kathrin Bylebyl |author2=Peter Poschlod |author3=Christoph Reisch |year=2008 |title=Genetic variation of ''Eryngium campestre'' L. (Apiaceae) in Central Europe |journal=Molecular Ecology |volume=17 |issue=14 |pages=3379–3388 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-294X.2008.03836.x |pmid=18564089 |bibcode=2008MolEc..17.3379B |s2cid=12782232 }}</ref> In the British Isles it is very uncommon in dry [[grassland]] on neutral or calcareous soils in the southeast, having first been recorded in 1662 by the naturalist [[John Ray]] in Devon. It has statutory protection in Somerset and Devon and is persisting in several sites there, but elsewhere it is mostly a short-lived casual of waste ground, road verges and rough pastures.<ref name=OnlineAtlas>{{cite web |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/eryngium-campestre |title=''Eryngium campestre'' |work=Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |accessdate=23 March 2020 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>

==Biology==
The [[leaf|leaves]] of this plant are mined by the [[gall fly]], ''[[Euleia heraclei]]''.<ref name=grid>{{cite web | url=https://data.nbn.org.uk/Taxa/NBNSYS0000012861/Grid_Map | title=Grid map of records on the Gateway for ''Euleia heraclei'' | publisher=National Biodiversity Network | year=2012 | accessdate=18 May 2012}}</ref>

==Uses==
It is used in herbalism as an infusion to treat coughs, [[whooping cough]] and urinary infections. Roots were formerly candied as sweets or boiled and roasted as a vegetable.<ref name=PFAF>{{cite web |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Eryngium+campestre |title=''Eryngium campestre'' |publisher=Plants For A Future |accessdate=23 March 2020}}</ref> The plant's active constituents are essential oils, [[saponin]]s, [[tannin]]s.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Murat Kartal |author2=Anne-Claire Mitaine-Offer |author3=Thomas Paululat |author4=Mahmoud Abu-Asaker |author5=Hildebert Wagner |author6=Jean-François Mirjolet |author7=Nicolas Guilbaud |author8=Marie-Aleth Lacaille-Dubois |year=2006 |title=Triterpene Saponins from ''Eryngium campestre'' |journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=69 |issue=7 |pages=1105–1108 |doi=10.1021/np060101w |pmid=16872157 }}</ref>

In Iran's [[Mazandaran Province]], it has been used in various local dishes for centuries.
